content: Chytridiomycosis is a lethal infectious disease that primarily affects amphibians. It is caused by the chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (commonly abbreviated as B. dendrobatidis). This disease has been strongly associated with significant population declines and even extinctions of amphibian species in regions such as western North America, Central America, South America, and eastern Australia. Currently, there are no effective strategies to control chytridiomycosis in wild amphibian populations. The disease is a major contributor to the global decline of amphibian populations, with approximately 30% of amphibian species worldwide being affected. While some population declines have been directly attributed to B. dendrobatidis, certain amphibian species exhibit resistance to the infection. Additionally, some reports indicate that certain populations can persist with low levels of the disease over time. Most laboratory studies on chytridiomycosis lack ecological relevance, which limits the applicability of their findings to real-world field conditions. The earliest documented cases of B. dendrobatidis infection were observed in African clawed frogs of the genus Xenopus. Since Xenopus frogs have been widely transported across the globe, they are considered a potential vector for the spread of B. dendrobatidis. However, other studies suggest that B. dendrobatidis has been present in North and Central America for decades, indicating that its spread may not be solely linked to the movement of Xenopus frogs. Laboratory research has shown that the chytrid fungus does not thrive at high temperatures. Exposing infected frogs to elevated temperatures has been demonstrated to kill the fungus. This temperature sensitivity may explain why chytridiomycosis is more prevalent in cooler climates.
